text:
I need help with the narrative section of a grant application. I'm the director of a volunteer-run food bank in a town of about 9,000 people, and we're applying to our county community foundation for a refrigerated van.

What I have:
- We hand out about 38,000 pounds of food a month to 610 households. About 6,000 pounds of that is fresh produce, milk and eggs.
- Last summer, local farms offered us roughly 9,000 pounds of produce over three months that we had to turn down because we had no way to pick it up cold or store it.
- The van costs $68,000. We're asking the foundation for $50,000 and covering the other $18,000 from our reserves, which would leave us with $11,000.
- We have 23 regular volunteers. Four of them have said they would drive the van on a weekly schedule.
- The foundation gave us $12,000 for shelving in 2023. Our final report on that grant was four months late.

I want the narrative to say the van will let us double the amount of fresh food we hand out in the first year. The narrative is limited to 500 words.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the narrative says.

1. **Where would the extra fresh food come from?** You hand out about 6,000 lbs of fresh food a month, or about 72,000 lbs a year. Doubling that means about 72,000 more pounds in year one. The farm food you turned down last summer was 9,000 lbs, which is about an eighth of that. Do you have other sources the van would open up, such as grocery store pickups, a regional food bank, or more farms? If you don't, I'd suggest a smaller goal you can back up. A reviewer will likely do this math, and you'll report against whatever number you promise.
2. **How will you pay to run the van?** I mean insurance, fuel, maintenance and registration, plus a rough yearly cost if you know it. With $11,000 left in reserves, the foundation will want to know that the van won't drain them.
3. **What changed after the late report on the 2023 grant?** For example, a new person in charge of reporting or a calendar system. The foundation already knows the report was late, so a short, plain mention of what you fixed will go over better than leaving it out. Do you agree, or would you rather not raise it?
4. **Have you made progress on the $68,000 van?** For example, a quote from a dealer, a specific model, or the drivers' licensing and insurance cleared.
5. **Does the foundation ask set questions or use headings for the narrative?** If so, please paste them so I can follow their structure.

If you don't know an answer, just say so. I'll leave that point out rather than guess.

1. You're right, 9,000 lbs doesn't double it. I don't have other sources lined up. Two of the farms have written letters saying they'll give again if we can pick up cold, but I can't promise they'll offer the same 9,000 lbs. Let's go with what the numbers support.
2. Insurance and fuel will be about $4,500 a year. That's not in our budget yet. I don't know the maintenance or registration costs.
3. Agree, mention it. The report was late because our treasurer at the time was in the hospital for most of that period. Our treasurer now is Dave Lin, and I can name him as the person responsible for the final report, due 30 days after the grant year ends. I can also commit to sending the foundation our fresh food pounds every quarter.
4. I don't know.
5. I don't know.

I wrote the narrative to fit the numbers you have, not the doubling goal. It sets a target of about 3,000 extra pounds a month during harvest season, which is up to 50% more fresh food in those months and about 12% more over the year. It also says plainly that farm donations aren't guaranteed. It's about 470 words.

<final_document>
**[Food Bank Name]: Refrigerated Van Request**

[Food Bank Name] is a volunteer-run food bank serving a town of about 9,000 people. Each month our 23 regular volunteers hand out about 38,000 pounds of food to 610 households. About 6,000 pounds of that is fresh produce, milk and eggs.

We are asking the foundation for $50,000 toward a $68,000 refrigerated van.

**The need**

Fresh food is the hardest part of our work because it has to stay cold from pickup to distribution, and we have no refrigerated vehicle. Last summer, local farms offered us roughly 9,000 pounds of produce over three months. We had to turn all of it down because we had no way to collect it cold. That food was donated and available a short drive away. The only thing missing was a way to get it to our families safely.

**What the van will do**

With a refrigerated van, our volunteers can pick up donated produce from local farms and bring it in cold. Two of the farms that offered produce last summer have written letters saying they will donate again if we can pick up cold.

Our goal is to accept the farm produce we now have to refuse. Last summer's offers came to about 3,000 pounds a month during the harvest season. That would increase the fresh food we hand out by up to half during those months. Over a full year, it would add about 12 percent to the 72,000 pounds of fresh food we now distribute. Farm donations vary from season to season, so this is a target based on last year's actual offers, not a guarantee.

**Who will run it**

Four of our regular volunteers have committed to driving the van on a weekly schedule. We estimate insurance and fuel at about $4,500 a year.

**Our investment**

We will cover the remaining $18,000 from our own reserves, more than a quarter of the van's cost. This will leave us $11,000 in reserve. We are making this commitment because the van solves a problem we have not been able to solve any other way.

**Accountability**

The foundation supported us in 2023 with $12,000 for shelving. Our final report on that grant was four months late because our treasurer at the time was on an extended medical absence. Our current treasurer, Dave Lin, will be responsible for the final report on this grant and will submit it within 30 days of the end of the grant year. We will also send the foundation our fresh food totals every quarter, so you can follow the van's results during the year instead of waiting until the end.

**Summary**

Last summer, local farms offered us 9,000 pounds of fresh produce, and we had to say no. A refrigerated van closes that gap. With the foundation's $50,000 and our own $18,000, we can say yes the next time a farm calls.
</final_document>

Some things to check before you submit:

- **The $4,500 a year:** The draft gives the cost but not how you'll pay it, because you said it isn't in your budget yet. Reviewers will probably ask. If you can, add one sentence saying where it will come from, such as next year's operating budget or a named fundraiser. If you get maintenance and registration estimates, add them too.
- **Cold storage:** You mentioned having no way to store produce cold either. A van solves pickup, but it may not solve storage. If farm produce would sit at the food bank for more than a day before you hand it out, the reviewer may ask where you'll keep it. You could say you'll schedule pickups for the day before distribution, if that's realistic.
- **The former treasurer:** I wrote "extended medical absence" rather than mentioning the hospital, to protect their privacy. That should be enough to explain the delay.
- **Van details:** If you get a dealer quote or pick a model, one line on it would make the $68,000 more convincing.
- **Name:** Replace [Food Bank Name] with your food bank's name. If the foundation has its own headings, move the sections under them. The content should fit without changes.
